text: Removal was not one event.
It ran for years and bent in cruel directions.
The hardest came in 1838, after Chicago itself was already a city, when militia forced about 859 Potawatomi out of Indiana and marched them to eastern Kansas.
The march began at Twin Lakes, near Plymouth, Indiana, and ended on the fourth of November along the Osage River, near present-day Osawatomie.
The route ran roughly 660 miles over 61 days.
More than forty people died on the way, most of them children, of typhoid and exhaustion.
A young priest, Father Benjamin Petit, walked the whole distance with them and kept a journal.
He never recovered.
He died the next year in St.
Louis, at twenty-seven.
History remembers that march as the Trail of Death.
The Potawatomi were scattered, not erased.

The bands that were marched to Kansas became the Prairie Band Potawatomi Nation, which in 2024 had a piece of its ancestral ground at Shabbona placed back in trust and became the first federally recognized tribe with land in Illinois.
One band never left at all.
Chief Leopold Pokagon kept about 280 people in southwestern Michigan, and by 1838 they had bought 874 acres of their own land near Dowagiac.
Their descendants are the Pokagon Band of Potawatomi, more than six thousand citizens today.
The people who held this lakefront are still here.
With the land legally cleared, the city at the river mouth took off.
Chicago was incorporated as a town in 1833, the same year as the treaty, with about three hundred residents.
By 1837 it was a city of more than four thousand.
Soldiers cut a channel through the sandbar and gave the river a real harbor.
Speculators bought and flipped the wet lots faster than anyone could build on them, until the panic of 1837 wiped out the easy money and a lot of the speculators with it.
